You can create a lifecycle rule to optimize your objects' storage\\ncosts throughout their lifetime.\\n\\nYou can define the scope of the lifecycle rule to all objects in your bucket or to\\nobjects\\nwith a shared prefix, certain object tags, or a certain object size.\\n\\nYou can specify one or more predefined actions for Amazon S3 to perform. There are\\ntwo types of\\nactions: *transition* and *expiration*. Transition actions define when objects transition to a storage\\nclass for less-frequently accessed objects. Expiration actions define when objects\\nare\\nremoved. The effect of these actions depends on the versioning state of your bucket\\nand\\nobjects. Transitions and expirations are asynchronous operations. Your S3 costs, however,\\nare updated as though transitions and expirations were immediate.\\n\\nAmazon S3 has a list of supported lifecycle transitions between storage classes. For\\nmore\\ninformation about which storage classes you can transition objects to and the constraints\\nof\\nobject size, minimum days, and cost considerations, see Supported transitions and related constraints.\\n\\nWhen you create a new S3 Lifecycle rule Amazon S3 applies a default behavior to your\\nLifecycle configuration that prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned.\\nYou can allow smaller objects to transition by adding an **Object size** filter that specifies a smaller size to each applicable rule. Additionally, you can\\nchange the default transition behavior so that objects smaller than 128 KB will transition\\nto S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive. To do this, use the\\noptional `x-amz-transition-object-size-minimum-default` header in a PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration request.\\n\\nThe effects of expiration actions are permanent. To prevent accidental deletion, we\\nrecommend that you take precautions, such as enabling S3 Versioning, S3 Object Lock, multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete, or S3 Replication.\\n\\nUnder **Review transition and expiration actions**, you can also review how the specified actions work on the lifecycle of\\ncurrent and noncurrent versions of objects.\\n\\nThere are per-request transition charges to move data into any supported S3 storage\\nclass\\nand charges to store the transitioned objects in the storage class. For details on\\npricing,\\nsee **Lifecycle Transition requests** pricing on the **Requests\\n& data retrievals** tab and **Storage pricing** on the\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-create-page.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Lifecycle configuration\",\"context\":\"# Lifecycle configuration\\n\\nA lifecycle configuration is an XML file that consists of a set of rules with predefined\\nactions. These are actions that you want Amazon S3 to perform on objects during their\\nlifetime so\\nthat they are stored cost-effectively.\\n\\nThere are two types of predefined actions: *transition*\\nand *expiration*. Transition actions define when objects\\ntransition to another storage class. Expiration actions define when objects expire.\\nYou can\\nexpire all objects or a subset of objects that have a specific key name prefix. Amazon\\nS3 deletes\\nexpired objects on your behalf.\\n\\nIn a lifecycle configuration, you can have up to 1,000 rules. You can create new lifecycle\\nrules here. Or, select a rule in the list and choose **Actions** to enable\\nor disable the rule.\\n\\nYou can use a lifecycle configuration to empty a bucket. To do so, your lifecycle\\nconfiguration must include current versions, noncurrent versions, delete markers,\\nand\\nincomplete multipart uploads.\\n\\nAmazon S3 also supports a bucket lifecycle rule to stop multipart uploads that don't\\nfinish\\nwithin a specified number of days after being initiated. This rule helps to further\\nminimize\\nyour storage costs\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-policies-page.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Lifecycle rule details\",\"context\":\"# Lifecycle rule details\\n\\nYou can configure Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules to store your objects cost-effectively\\nthroughout their lifetime. You can instruct Amazon S3 to transition objects to less-expensive\\nstorage classes or to archive or delete objects.\\n\\nUse this page to see the scope of the selected S3 Lifecycle rule. You can also view\\ntransition and expiration actions for current and noncurrent object versions, based\\non your\\nlifecycle rule.\\n\\nFor **Current version actions**, you can see the following\\ninformation:\\n\\n* Since object creation, *the number of days* after\\n which a current version will be transitioned and *the storage\\n class* to transition that version to.\\n* Since object creation, *the number of days* after\\n which a current version will be expired.\\n\\nFor **Noncurrent versions actions**, you can see the following\\ninformation:\\n\\n* Since an object became noncurrent, *the number of\\n days* after which a noncurrent version will be transitioned and\\n *the storage class* to transition that version\\n to.\\n* After the transition, *the number of newest noncurrent\\n versions* to retain.\\n* Since an object became noncurrent, *the number of\\n days* to permanent deletion and *the number of\\n newest noncurrent versions* to retain afterward.\\n\\nUnder **Delete expired object delete markers or incomplete multipart\\nuploads**, there are two sections of configuration information:\\n\\n* You can see if your lifecycle rule is configured to delete expired object delete\\n markers. An expired object delete marker occurs when all object versions are\\n deleted, and only a single delete marker remains. If you selected this option in\\n your lifecycle rule, an expired object delete marker will be deleted.\\n* You can also see if your lifecycle rule deletes incomplete multipart uploads after\\n a specified number of days\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-view-page.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify S3 lifecycle rule cost-saving details in AWS docs"}

{"id": "c1c4c216-f86f-4be1-b239-afa94597484c", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "S3 Lifecycle rules cut cost in a few ways. Which ones fit depends on how your data is accessed.

## 1. Move data to cheaper storage classes (transition actions)
Move objects to cheaper classes as they age and are read less often. A typical path looks like this:
- **S3 Standard → Standard-IA or One Zone-IA** after about 30 days, for data you read occasionally.
- **→ Glacier Instant Retrieval** for archive data that still needs millisecond access.
- **→ Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive** for long-term retention. This is the cheapest option, but retrieval takes minutes to hours.

Check these before you add a transition:
- **Object size:** by default, Lifecycle won't transition objects smaller than 128 KB. You can override this with an object size filter. Per-request transition charges often outweigh the savings on lots of tiny objects.
- **Minimum storage durations:** the IA and Glacier classes bill a minimum number of days. For example, IA classes bill 30 days and Deep Archive bills 180. Transitioning data that you'll delete soon can cost more than leaving it in Standard.
- **Transition request charges:** each object moved incurs a per-request fee. Buckets with millions of small objects need a cost estimate first.
- **Retrieval fees:** these apply to IA and Glacier classes. Don't tier data that's still read often.

## 2. Expire data you no longer need (expiration actions)
- Delete logs, temp files, and build artifacts after their retention period. You can scope a rule by prefix, tag, or object size.
- Expiration is permanent, so make sure your retention and compliance requirements allow it.

## 3. Clean up hidden costs
These are often the easiest savings:
- **Abort incomplete multipart uploads** after 7 days or so. Orphaned parts are billed but don't show up as normal objects.
- **Expire noncurrent versions** on versioned buckets. Old versions pile up silently. You can keep only the newest N noncurrent versions, or delete them after a number of days.
- **Remove expired object delete markers** so they don't accumulate.

## 4. Example rule (JSON)
```json
{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "tier-and-clean-logs",
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
        { "Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
      ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 365 },
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30, "NewerNoncurrentVersions": 3 },
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}
```
You can apply it with `aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration`. Note that this call replaces the bucket's whole existing configuration, so merge in your current rules first.

## 5. Find what to target
- **S3 Storage Lens** or **Storage Class Analysis** show which prefixes are cold and which buckets carry the most noncurrent versions or incomplete uploads.
- **S3 Intelligent-Tiering** suits data with unpredictable access patterns. It moves objects between tiers automatically, with no retrieval fees. You can also use a lifecycle rule to transition objects into it.
- Test rules on a single prefix first, and use versioning, replication, or Object Lock as a safety net before you add expiration.

I can look at your actual buckets in this account. I'd check which have versioning enabled, which have lifecycle rules, and which have lots of old or incomplete data. Tell me if you want that, and which buckets or regions to cover.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
